title: Packages and crates
summary: What a crate is, binary versus library crates, the crate root, what a package contains, and how Cargo finds your crates by convention.

blocks.md:
So far every program has fit in one file. Real projects grow to thousands of lines, and some are split into many projects that depend on each other. Rust's **module system** is how you organize that code: what goes where, what other code can see, and how names are found. It has four layers:

- **Packages**: a Cargo feature for building, testing and sharing crates.
- **Crates**: a tree of modules that compiles to one library or executable.
- **Modules** and **use**: organize code inside a crate and control privacy.
- **Paths**: the way to name an item, such as a struct, function or module.

This lesson covers the first two. The rest of the chapter covers modules and paths.

blocks.title: Crates
blocks.md:
A **crate** is the smallest amount of code the Rust compiler considers at a time. Even `rustc main.rs` on a single file compiles a crate. A crate comes in one of two forms:

- A **binary crate** compiles to a program you can run. It must have a `main` function. Everything you have written so far is a binary crate.
- A **library crate** has no `main` and does not compile to a program. It defines functionality meant to be shared with other projects. The `rand` crate from chapter 2 is a library crate, and so are the exercises in this course: the tests are the code that uses them.

When Rust programmers say "crate" they usually mean a library crate, and "crate" is used interchangeably with "library".

The **crate root** is the source file the compiler starts from. It forms the root module of the crate, and every other module hangs from it.

blocks.title: Packages
blocks.md:
A **package** is a bundle of one or more crates with a `Cargo.toml` that describes how to build them. A package can contain any number of binary crates, but **at most one** library crate. It must contain at least one crate of either kind.

Cargo finds crates by convention, so `Cargo.toml` does not need to list them:

blocks.title: Where Cargo looks
rows: the binary crate with the same name as the package
the library crate with the same name as the package
one extra binary crate per file
integration tests: each file is a separate crate that uses your library (chapter 11)
example programs, run with `cargo run --example name`

blocks.title: A package with a library and two programs
blocks.code:
$ cargo new --lib satellites
$ tree satellites
satellites
├── Cargo.toml
└── src
    ├── bin
    │   └── groundctl.rs      # binary crate "groundctl"
    ├── lib.rs                # library crate "satellites" (crate root)
    └── main.rs               # binary crate "satellites"
blocks.explain: `cargo new --lib` starts a package with only `src/lib.rs`; the other two files were added by hand. A common, useful layout is a thin `main.rs` that parses arguments and calls into `lib.rs`, where the real logic lives and can be tested. Chapter 12 builds a program that way.

blocks.title: Editions are per crate
blocks.md: The `edition = "2024"` line in `Cargo.toml` applies to that package's crates only. A 2024-edition crate can depend on a 2015-edition crate and the other way round, so the ecosystem never splits when new editions arrive. *Programming Rust* calls this one of Rust's strongest compatibility promises.

questions.q: Which is true of a library crate?
options: It compiles to a program you can run
It defines functionality for other code to use and has no `main`
questions.explanation: A package has at most one library crate, and it has no `main`.

questions.q: A package has `src/main.rs`, `src/lib.rs` and `src/bin/tool.rs`. How many crates is that?
questions.explanation: Two binaries (the package name and `tool`) plus one library.

questions.q: The source file the compiler starts from, which forms the root module of a crate, is called the crate ______.
A 2024-edition crate cannot use a library written in the 2018 edition.
questions.explanation: Editions are chosen per crate and crates of different editions work together.

points: A crate is one unit of compilation: a binary (has `main`) or a library (does not).
The crate root (`src/main.rs` or `src/lib.rs`) is where compilation starts.
A package is a `Cargo.toml` plus one or more crates: any number of binaries, at most one library.
Cargo finds crates by file location; extra binaries go in `src/bin/`.
Editions are chosen per crate, so crates of different editions mix freely.

terms.def: The unit the compiler works on: a tree of modules that compiles to one library or one executable.
A crate with a main function that compiles to an executable.
A crate without main that provides code for other crates to use.
The source file the compiler starts from and the root module of the crate.
One or more crates plus a Cargo.toml describing how to build them; at most one library crate.
